paras: The lynching of George Beckett took place at Aberdeen, Monroe County, Mississippi, early on the morning of June 2, 1882, when a crowd took Beckett, a Black man, from the county jail and hanged him. He had been accused of attempting to outrage a girl of about seven years old. The case reached papers across the country ten days later through a St. Louis Post-Dispatch wire that misdated it to June 11, and was paired in news digests with lynchings at Rock Hill, South Carolina, and Lawrence, Kansas.

According to a special dispatch from Aberdeen to the Memphis Daily Appeal, word reached the town at 7 o'clock on Thursday evening, June 1, that an outrage had been attempted on the young daughter of "one of our respected citizens." Inquiry pointed to Beckett, whom the correspondent called "the fiend." The wire version named the girl's father as "Agnew" or "Arknew" and described him as a white man.

In the Aberdeen account, officers arrested Beckett after he resisted, and he was wounded by a pistol shot before he was lodged in jail. The Post-Dispatch wire told the capture differently: a party of citizens with shotguns and bloodhounds ran him down near the Tombigbee River and fired on him when he refused to surrender, wounding him seriously. Both versions agree that he was jailed after being shot.

Crowds gathered around the jail through the evening, and the officers' efforts to calm them failed. At half past one in the morning a crowd of 200 took possession of the jail, some of them seizing and holding the jailer while others took Beckett a few yards away and hanged him from the gallows on which Jones and Miller, convicted of murdering the Walker brothers, had been executed. The wire reports instead said he was hanged to the limb of a tree, and a National Associated Press dispatch said "vigilantes" hanged him at midnight from a projecting beam of a blacksmith shop.

No report of an inquest, arrests or any official response appears in the coverage. Mississippi papers treated the hanging as settled news: the Jackson Weekly Clarion said Beckett was jailed "and then hung," and The Comet of Jackson noted on June 10 that he had been hung at Aberdeen "recently."

The first report, the Aberdeen special in the Memphis Daily Appeal of June 3, ran under the headline "A Negro Brute Hanged by a Mob" and called Beckett "this vile monster." Its closing line conceded that "such acts of lawlessness are to be deplored" but declared that "the course of Judge Lynch is heartily approved." The Clarion condensed the same text for its state-news column, and the Greenville Times reprinted it with credit on June 17.

On June 13 the Post-Dispatch wire from Jackson appeared in the Sacramento Daily Record-Union, the Memphis Daily Appeal itself and other dailies, followed by the Grenada Sentinel and the Somerset Herald. Headlines such as "Lynching a Villain" and "Hanging a Negro Ravisher" took the charge as proven, and the dispatch called Beckett "the brute." Copies garbled the details as they spread: one misspelled the father's name as "Norhaust" and placed him in "Marion county," and digest lines put the jail "at Jackson."

Weekly papers in the North and West carried the case as one line in national digests. The Kenosha Telegraph placed it beside a meeting of Black residents at Lawrence denouncing the lynching there, and the Hand County Press counted it among three lynchings "in one day last week." Kentucky papers ran an unnamed version in which a "wretch" was run down with bloodhounds and hanged.

The date is the main conflict: the Aberdeen special, printed June 3, puts the hanging at 1:30 a.m. on the morning after a Thursday evening arrest, while the June 12 wire dispatches say the assault took place "yesterday," a Sunday, and the hanging that night. The local account is the better evidence: it was in print by June 3, and The Comet reported the hanging as past on June 10. Accounts also differ on whether officers or an armed party with bloodhounds caught him, and on whether he was hanged from the jail gallows, a tree or a blacksmith shop beam.

reader.title: Lynching of George Beckett
bases: A crowd seized the jailer and took Beckett, a Black man held on a charge of attempted outrage, from the Monroe County jail and hanged him (A1, A5, A10).
Every report says he was hanged by a crowd or mob (A1 gives 200) that took him from jail over the jailer's resistance, in punishment for an alleged attempted outrage on a child (A1, A5, A10).

The Aberdeen special (A1), the Jackson papers (A2, A3) and the separate Post-Dispatch and National Associated Press wires (A5, A7) all report the same victim, charge, wounding, jailing and mob hanging, though they differ on date and details.

accounts.label: Aberdeen special to the Memphis Appeal
accounts.gist: Officers arrested Beckett Thursday evening after resistance in which he was shot; at 1:30 a.m. a crowd of 200 held the jailer and hanged him from the jail gallows used for an earlier legal execution.

accounts.label: St. Louis Post-Dispatch wire from Jackson, June 12
accounts.gist: Citizens with shotguns and bloodhounds ran Beckett down near the Tombigbee River and shot him when he refused to surrender; jailed under guard, he was taken out that night by a crowd that overpowered the jailer and hanged to a tree limb.

accounts.label: National Associated Press wire from Jackson, June 12
accounts.gist: 'Vigilantes' took 'George Becker' from jail at midnight and hanged him to a projecting beam of a blacksmith shop.

framing.detail: The Memphis Appeal's Aberdeen correspondent called Beckett 'the fiend' and 'this vile monster' and wrote that 'the course of Judge Lynch is heartily approved.'
Wire headlines read 'Lynching a Villain' and 'Hanging a Negro Ravisher', and the dispatch called him 'the brute'.
Northern and western papers ran short digest items pairing the case with the Rock Hill, S.C., and Lawrence, Kan., lynchings.

versions.value: Thursday evening and 1:30 a.m. the next morning (about June 1-2)

conflicts.note: The Aberdeen special was printed June 3, and The Comet (Jackson) reported him already hung on June 10, so the hanging cannot have taken place on June 11; the June 12 wire appears to be a late rewrite of the same event that took 'yesterday' from its own dateline.
